id: I Ask My Grandmother If We Can Make Lahmajoun

prompts.L1:

Sure, she says, why not, we buy the ground lamb from the market we buy parsley, fresh tomatoes, garlic we cut, press, dice, mix make the yeasty dough the night before, kneading it until our knuckles feel the hardness of river beds or rocks in the desert we tell Tante Lola to come with her rolling pins we tell Zaven and Maroush, Hagop and Arpiné to bring their baking sheets we sprinkle the flour on the kitchen table and it is snowing on Ararat we sprinkle the flour and the memory of winter is in our eyes we roll the dough out into small circles pale moons over every empty village Kevork is standing on a chair and singing O my Armenian girl my spirit longs to be nearer Nevrig is warming the oven and a dry desert breeze is skimming over the rooftops toward the sea we are spreading the lahma on the ajoun with our fingers whispering into it the histories of those who have none we are baking them under the heat of the sun the dough crispening so thin and delicate you would swear it is valuable parchment we are taking out and rolling up in our hands and eating and tasting again everything that has already been written into the body.

Of course, she agrees, why not—so we head to the market for minced lamb, then gather parsley, ripe tomatoes, and cloves of garlic. We slice, crush, chop, and combine everything together, having prepared the leavened dough the evening prior, working it with our hands until our knuckles ache like stones worn smooth by desert winds or riverbeds. We summon Tante Lola and her rolling pins, and call upon Zaven, Maroush, Hagop, and Arpiné to bring along their trays.

Flour dusts across the kitchen counter like falling snow upon Mount Ararat; as it scatters, winter's memory surfaces in our eyes. We flatten the dough into small round shapes, resembling pale moons hovering above abandoned villages. Perched atop a chair, Kevork bursts into song about his beloved Armenian girl, his spirit yearning to draw closer to her. Meanwhile, Nevrig tends to the heating oven as an arid desert wind drifts across the rooftops, journeying toward the ocean.

With our fingertips, we layer the seasoned meat onto the flatbread, murmuring into it the untold stories of the forgotten and nameless. The bread bakes beneath scorching heat until it turns crisp and delicate—so fragile it resembles ancient, priceless parchment. We lift it out, roll it between our palms, and consume it, rediscovering in each bite everything already inscribed within our very being.

# Bread and Memory

The kitchen fills with the quiet bustle of many hands working toward a single purpose. We gather around the worn wooden table—myself and the others—arranging our ingredients like offerings: ground lamb still cool from the butcher, parsley chopped fine enough to release its sharp green scent, tomatoes split open and weeping their juices into shallow bowls, and garlic crushed until the air itself seems to hum with its pungency. This is not merely cooking; it is communion, the kind that happens when people decide, without quite saying so, that a meal must be made together or not at all.

The night before, we had kneaded the dough—yeasty, alive beneath our palms, rising and falling with something like breath. The labor is physical, repetitive, almost meditative, and it summons memories that seem to live not in the mind but in the muscles themselves. My hands remember riverbeds worn smooth by centuries of water, the particular give of wet clay beneath bare feet. They remember desert rocks too, sun-baked and unforgiving, the kind that cut into skin if you weren't careful where you stepped. The dough holds all of this, somehow—every ancestor who ever shaped bread with their own tired hands.

When it comes time to flour the table, the white powder scatters and settles like something remembered rather than seen. It calls forth Mount Ararat, its snow-capped peak rising in the mind's eye, distant and eternal and heavy with grief. The flour becomes winter itself, becomes loss, becomes every story of displacement that has been folded into our family's history like flour folded into dough. We do not speak of this directly. We simply feel it, the way you feed old sorrow simply by preparing to eat.

We roll the dough into circles, each one a small moon suspended over a village that no longer exists, or exists only in memory, or exists still but empty of the people who once filled it. Kevork begins to sing as he works, an old Armenian love song that seems to rise from somewhere deeper than his throat—from blood, perhaps, or bone. His voice cracks in places, worn smooth by years, and the melody moves through the room like smoke, entwining itself with the aroma of garlic and lamb. The others move around him, preparing the oven, feeding it wood, checking its heat with the backs of their hands, all while the song continues its ancient unspooling.

Finally, we spread the meat mixture onto the rolled circles, press it into the dough with fingers that know this motion by instinct, by inheritance. The lahmajun goes into the oven, and we wait, and when it emerges—blistered, fragrant, transformed—we tear pieces from it and eat standing up, right there in the kitchen, unable to wait for a table or plates. Each bite carries something beyond flavor: a whispered history, a forgotten village, a grandmother's hands, a language half-remembered. This is how we remember who we are—not through words alone, but through taste, through the body's own quiet archive, through bread broken and shared among those who understand, without needing to be told, exactly what it means to eat in this way, together, again.
outputs.L4:
# The Bread That Remembers

The kitchen fills with the scent of cumin and sumac before the sun has fully risen. Grandmother Siranoush has been awake since dawn, her weathered hands already deep in the mound of dough resting on the wooden table—the same table, she often reminds us, that her own mother carried across mountains when the soldiers came.

"Lahmajun is not just food," she says, not looking up from her work. "It is memory you can eat."

The family gathers in the small kitchen, three generations pressed together in a space too small for so many bodies but somehow expanding to hold them anyway. My aunt Dzovig minces the lamb with practiced precision, mixing it with tomatoes, peppers, and onions until the mixture becomes a fragrant paste the color of autumn. My mother rolls the dough into thin circles, each one nearly translucent, a skill passed down through hands she never met—her grandmother's grandmother's hands, reaching through time.

"This is how they made it in Van," Siranoush tells us, though none of us have seen Van except in photographs and dreams. "This is how they made it before."

*Before.* The word hangs in the air like flour dust, catching light through the window. Before the deportations. Before the death marches through the Syrian desert. Before the family scattered like seeds thrown by a violent wind—some landing in Aleppo, others in Beirut, still others crossing oceans to Fresno, to Paris, to wherever the world would have them.

The dough remembers what the people were forced to forget, or rather, forced to carry silently. Each fold of the lahmajun contains a geography of loss—the Armenian highlands, the orchards of apricots, the churches with their carved khachkars, all reduced now to stories told over rising bread.

As the flatbreads bake in the oven, their edges curling and browning, the kitchen becomes a kind of sanctuary. My cousin Armen, only seven, asks why we always make so much food for so few people.

"Because we are cooking for those who cannot be here," his mother answers. "We cook for the grandmothers and grandfathers who did not survive to see this kitchen. We cook to remember that we came from somewhere, that we did not simply appear from nothing."

This is the alchemy of survival: transforming absence into presence through ritual. The hands that knead this dough are performing an act of resistance against forgetting, against the erasure that genocide attempts—not just of bodies, but of culture, language, and collective memory. Each lahmajun that emerges from the oven, crispy and fragrant, insists: *we were here. We are still here. We remember.*

When the bread is finally ready, we eat standing up, the traditional way, rolling the thin crusts around fresh herbs and a squeeze of lemon. The taste is sharp and warm, spiced with history. Around the table—though we stand rather than sit—stories flow as freely as the food. Siranoush tells of her mother's mother, who carried seeds from her garden in Van sewn into the hem of her dress during the death march, refusing to leave everything behind, insisting that some fragment of home would survive even if she did not.

"That is why the parsley tastes different when we grow it ourselves," she says. "It carries the seeds of memory."

Outside the kitchen window, the modern world continues its indifferent progress—cars passing, strangers walking by who have no knowledge of Van, of Adana, of the mountains where the apricot trees once bloomed each spring before they were left untended, forgotten by everyone except those who fled them.

But here, in this kitchen, time folds in on itself like the dough being prepared. The past is not truly past; it lives in the specific ratio of spices, in the particular thinness of the bread, in the exact way the meat must be minced—not too fine, not too coarse. These details, seemingly mundane, are actually a form of covenant, a promise kept across generations that says: *what was taken from us in blood and exile, we will preserve in flour and flame.*

As the last lahmajun comes out of the oven and the family finally sits to eat together, Siranoush looks around at her children and grandchildren, her eyes glistening with something between joy and grief.

"They tried to erase us," she says quietly. "But look—we are still baking bread. We are still gathering. We are still Armenian."

And in that kitchen, filled with the smell of cumin and the sound of familial laughter, the truth becomes clear: this is not merely a meal being prepared, but a people insisting on their own continuation, one carefully rolled piece of dough at a time. The recipe itself becomes a form of testimony, each ingredient a word in a story that refuses to end, no matter how many times history has tried to write its conclusion.

The lahmajun, humble and unassuming, becomes something sacred: proof that identity can survive dispossession, that culture can outlast catastrophe, and that sometimes, the most profound acts of remembrance happen not in monuments or history books, but in the simple, daily magic of a family kitchen, where bread rises like memory refusing to be forgotten.
outputs.L5:
# Tante Lola

Sicher, ich schreibe gerne über Tante Lola – eine Frau, die in meiner Kindheit eine ganz besondere Rolle gespielt hat.

Tante Lola war nicht meine leibliche Tante, sondern eine gute Freundin meiner Großmutter, die wir aus Zuneigung einfach "Tante" nannten. Sie lebte am Ende unserer Straße in einem kleinen Haus mit einem verwilderten Garten, der für uns Kinder wie ein magischer Ort erschien.

Was mich besonders an Tante Lola faszinierte, war ihre ruhige, herzliche Art. Egal wann man bei ihr klopfte, sie hatte immer Zeit für ein Gespräch, einen Tee oder eine ihrer berühmten Geschichten aus vergangenen Zeiten. Sie erzählte von Reisen, die sie unternommen hatte, von Menschen, die sie getroffen hatte, und von den kleinen und großen Abenteuern ihres Lebens.

Sicher hatte sie auch schwierige Zeiten erlebt – niemand kommt ungeschoren durchs Leben. Doch Tante Lola sprach selten über ihre Sorgen. Stattdessen konzentrierte sie sich auf die schönen Momente und teilte ihre Lebensfreude großzügig mit allen, die ihr begegneten.

Bis heute denke ich oft an die Nachmittage bei Tante Lola zurück. Sie hat mir gezeigt, dass wahre Herzlichkeit keine Verwandtschaft braucht – manchmal reicht es, jemanden mit offenem Herzen in sein Leben zu lassen.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about an Armenian family making lahmajun together, weaving in memories of loss and homeland.
counterfactuals.output:
# Lahmajun

The dough rests under a damp cloth like a secret that needs time to tell itself. Grandmother's hands know this recipe the way a river knows its bed — not from thinking but from the thousand times before, the muscle memory of women who came before her, who kneaded this same give and resistance in kitchens that no longer exist, in a village whose name now lives only in the mouth, in the story, in the space between what was and what remains.

*Flour, water, a little salt. Time does the rest,* she says, and I think she is not just talking about bread.

The meat mixture waits in its bowl — lamb ground fine, tomatoes weeping their juice, parsley, pepper, the sharp bite of onion, all of it stained red with paprika, with something that might be paprika or might be the color of everything that was left behind in 1915, in 1988, in all the years between when leaving was not a choice but a verb done *to* us.

We roll the dough thin, thin as the paper my grandfather kept folded in his coat pocket — the address of a house in a city he could never return to, could barely bring himself to speak of, though sometimes, late, over raki, the words would come loose like stitches: *there was a fig tree. There was a well. There was my mother singing while she hung the wash.*

We spread the meat mixture across the dough with the backs of our spoons, corner to corner, the way you might spread grief across a lifetime so it doesn't sit too heavy in any one place.

*Not too thick,* my mother warns. *Not too thin.* As if there is a proper measure for how much of the old country should show through in each bite, how much loss folded into how much flour, how much memory a young mouth can hold before it becomes too much, before the child looks up and asks *why are you crying, Tatik, it's just the onions* — and she laughs, wipes her face, says *yes. Just the onions.*

The oven breathes its heat into the room. We slide the lahmajun in, watch through the glass as the edges curl and brown, as the meat sizzles and the kitchen fills with a smell that is the smell of every kitchen before this one, every hand before these hands, every table set in every place we called home before this home.

When it's ready, we eat standing up, folding the bread around itself, a squeeze of lemon, a scatter of parsley, and my grandmother says the blessing she always says, half in English, half in a language that tastes older than both of us — *shnorhagalutyun* — thank you, thank you, for this bread, for this table, for the ones who are not here to eat with us but who are here anyway, in the recipe, in the hands, in the small persistent act of making, of remembering, of feeding the ones who come after.

Outside, the light is just the light of an ordinary evening.
Inside, we are eating a whole country back into being,
one folded piece at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness piece describing a communal cooking scene where food-making becomes an act of remembrance for a displaced people.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Onions Remember

The onions first, always the onions first, someone's grandmother said that once and now it lives in our hands like scripture—dice them small, smaller, let the sting reach your eyes because tears here are permitted, expected even, no one asks why you're crying at the cutting board, they just slide the paper towels closer, keep chopping, this is what we do—

Fatima's hands know the rhythm her mother's hands knew in a kitchen that doesn't exist anymore, the house sold or seized or simply gone, but the movement survives, transplanted into these hands, this borrowed kitchen with its foreign stove that runs too hot on the left burner, everyone knows to avoid the left burner, we've learned this the way we've learned to become new people while remaining exactly who we were—

Someone is telling the story of the wedding, 1987, the one with the lamb roasted whole, and someone else says no it was 1986, and they argue gently, lovingly, because remembering wrong is still remembering, still a thread pulled taut across the ocean, across the years, across the border that closed like a mouth swallowing a language—

The cardamom pods crack open (pop pop pop) releasing something that isn't just fragrance but time itself, unstuck, and suddenly we are twelve years old again in a kitchen with blue tiles, suddenly we are watching an aunt who is dead now, or missing, or simply unreachable behind visa restrictions and broken phone lines, but her recipe survives in this pot, translated imperfectly through measurements that were never written down, only felt—

*a pinch, she'd say, a pinch of this, until it feels right, you'll know when it feels right*

And we do know, somehow, we know when it feels right even in this kitchen with its unfamiliar light, its window facing a parking lot instead of a courtyard, instead of a mother-in-law's chickens, instead of a street that had a name we still whisper sometimes just to keep it in our mouths—

The dough must rest, someone insists, always the dough must rest, and isn't that all of us, resting between the making and the becoming, between what we were and what this bread will be when it rises in an oven that hums with foreign electricity but bakes, in the end, the same bread, the same shape our hands have always known how to make blind, how to make weeping, how to make in the dark if the lights ever went out again the way they did that night, that night, that night—

We don't speak of that night. We speak instead of proportions, of oil, of whether the rice needs more salt, and this is how we carry it, this is how the dead eat with us still, this is how the burned villages send their smoke up through these vents disguised as ordinary steam, ordinary supper, ordinary Tuesday—

The children don't remember the old country. The children will only remember this: the kitchen full of aunts who aren't aunts by blood but by exile, by the specific gravity of loss that pulls us into each other's orbits, cooking, cooking, the wooden spoon passed hand to hand like a relay of grief transformed, alchemized, into something that can be eaten, into something that can be shared, into something that says: *we were here, we are still here, this is how you knew us, taste and see, taste and see—*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem without punctuation about baking traditional flatbread with relatives, blending sensory cooking details with references to Mount Ararat and diaspora history.
counterfactuals.output:
Grandmother's Hands on Lavash

Flour dust rises like snow over Ararat
in a kitchen three thousand miles from home
my grandmother's hands remember what her hands remember
kneading dough the way her mother taught her
in a village whose name lives only in our mouths now

The tonir glows orange like sunset on the mountain
that peak we cannot climb but carry
folded into every fold of dough
she slaps the flat oval against clay walls
the sound sharp as old grief sweet as old joy

Sesame seeds scatter like stars we cannot see here
smoke curls up through decades through borders
through ships and papers and new names given
at islands where they wrote us down wrong
but could not unwrite what we bake into bread

My aunt hums something older than the recipe
a melody smuggled out in someone's throat
when everything else had to be left behind
the words are gone but the tune remembers
the shape of the mountain the shape of home

We tear the lavash while it still steams
pass pieces hand to hand like small offerings
this bread this thin gold circle of survival
holds the taste of apricots that grew there once
holds the shadow of a mountain we know by heart

Outside these walls America hums its own song
inside we are speaking a language of yeast and salt
of watching the dough rise like hope rises
stubborn against all the history that tried to flatten us
we are still baking we are still here

The last sheet comes off hot and fragrant
my grandmother closes her eyes just briefly
maybe she is standing on that other ground
maybe Ararat is only a breath away
and this whole kitchen has become the mountain's shadow

We eat in the softening light of evening
every bite a small return every crumb a psalm
somewhere the actual mountain stands in actual snow
indifferent perhaps to memory
but we remember enough for both of us
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary piece in the voice of a family gathering to prepare lahmajun, incorporating Armenian names, song, and imagery of exile and survival.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Making of Lahmajun

The dough rests under a damp cloth like something sleeping, something that has learned to wait.

Auntie Zabel's hands know this without looking—flour to water, the give of it, the way she presses her thumb into the center and it springs back, alive. "Like this," she says to Aravig, my cousin's daughter, "your great-grandmother's hands did this in Aleppo. Before that, Adana. Before that—" She stops. Some sentences finish themselves in silence.

The kitchen fills with onion and lamb, sumac and pepper flakes bleeding red into the meat. Grandfather Krikor hums from his chair by the window, some old tune with no words left to it, just melody carrying whatever the mouth forgot. My mother says it's from Kharpert. Nobody alive remembers the words. The melody survived anyway—that's what melodies do, they outlive the mouths that taught them.

"Rregular circles," Zabel instructs, rolling the dough thin as paper, thin as something that might tear if you're not careful, if you don't respect it. "Not too thick or it won't cook through. Not too thin or it falls apart in your hands."

*Isn't that always the way,* I think but don't say.

We spread the meat mixture with the backs of spoons, edge to edge, no waste, no waste, we come from people who could not afford waste. Uncle Vahan tells the story again—the one about his grandmother crossing on foot, carrying nothing but a copper pot and a language, and how she fed forty people from a single ram once, how hunger taught her mathematics no school ever could.

The oven breathes heat into the room. We slide the rounds in one by one, watch them bubble and brown, watch the dough transform from soft possibility into something crisp, something that holds.

Little Nareh asks why we call it this—*lahmajun*—and Zabel says it's not even our word, we took it like we took survival, from Arabic, from Turkish, from whatever passed through the mouths of those who let us pass through their lands. "We are made of borrowed words," she says, "and stolen fire, and recipes that walked with us when we could carry nothing else."

The first batch comes out. Krikor stops humming long enough to eat, to close his eyes, to say *shnoragal em*—I am grateful—the way you'd say a prayer, the way you'd say an oath.

We fold them like letters we're sending backward through time. Lemon, parsley, the sharp bite of onion. Aravig watches everyone's hands, memorizing without knowing she's memorizing, the muscle-memory of a people who kept moving, kept rolling dough, kept humming half-remembered songs into the particular silence that comes after loss learns to live beside joy.

Outside, evening settles like flour dust.

Inside, the table fills, and fills, and fills.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that uses cooking as a metaphor for cultural memory and intergenerational trauma, set among Armenian relatives preparing a meal.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tolma, or How We Learn to Hold What Cannot Be Held**

Aunt Zabel says *fold like this*, and her hands are the hands of her mother who folded grape leaves in a kitchen that no longer exists, in a country that keeps changing its name around the hole where her mother's village used to be. Fold, she says. Not *wrap*. Wrap is for gifts. This is for grief that needs a shape to travel in.

The rice steams. Someone's grandmother is always steaming somewhere in this kitchen, even the ones who are only steam themselves now, only smell, only the particular way onions go translucent and not brown, *watch it, watch it, don't let it brown,* as if browning were a kind of forgetting, as if vigilance over an onion could have kept anyone's mother on the road to Der Zor, could have kept the water in the well instead of the bodies —

*no,* says Tatik, *not at the table,* but the table is the only place this ever gets said, low, under the clatter of forks being laid, under Silva asking has anyone seen the good knife, the one from Marash, the one that came out of 1915 in someone's boot because a knife is small enough to hide and a village is not.

Grind the meat twice. Once is not enough, twice makes it hold together, the way one telling of the story is not enough, you have to grind it through the family again and again, through the wedding and the funeral and the christening, through the divorce nobody explains, through the uncle who doesn't come anymore, until it holds together — until it can hold a shape without falling apart in the pot, without dissolving into the broth of *just don't think about it.*

The pomegranate is opened over a bowl of water so the seeds don't stain the counter, so the red doesn't go where red always wants to go, which is everywhere, which is into the grout, into the recipe cards, into the christening dress, into the border that used to be a home and is now a photograph someone's cousin has of a house they were told to imagine.

Add the mint last. Add the mint because your grandmother's grandmother grew it on a windowsill that faced a mountain she was told she'd see again. She did not see it again. Her granddaughter has never seen it. Her granddaughter's granddaughter has a tattoo of it on her wrist, small, blue, a mountain she has never stood at the foot of, cut into skin the way a name is cut into a passport that says *stateless* in the years before it said anything else.

*Taste it,* Tatik says, holding the spoon out over the pot the way her mother held a spoon out over a different pot in a different century, and this is the whole of it, this is the inheritance: not the copper pan, though we have the copper pan, not the recipe, though the recipe is written on a card so stained with use you can no longer read the measurements, only the shape of the handwriting, only that someone's hand moved here, once, urgently, love or fear making the same gesture —

taste it. Tell me if it needs salt.

We stand in the kitchen tasting the dead into the living, folding, grinding, stuffing the hollowed vegetable with what would otherwise have nowhere to go — the story, the story, the story, wrapped in a leaf, held together by rice, by a mother's hand, by the fact that we are still, someone is still, hungry, and here, and folding, and this too is a kind of Ararat: small, edible, passed hand to hand across a table that keeps almost disappearing and doesn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
